snippet: Darwin Godel Machine: Open-Ended Evolution of Self-Improving Agents | Hacker News | Darwin Godel Machine: Open-Ended Evolution of Self-Improving Agents(arxiv.org) | | --- | | 55 points by tzury 8 months ago| hide| past| favorite| 16 comments | I recently did a deep dive on open-endedness, and my favorite example of its power is Picbreeder from 2008 [1]. It was a simple website where users could somewhat arbitrarily combine pictures created by super simple NNs. Most images were garbage, but a few resembled real objects. The best part is that attempts to replicate these by a traditional hill-climbing method would result in drastically more complicated solutions or even no solution at all. It's a helpful analogy to understand the contrast between today's gradient descent vs open-ended exploration. the same thing is at work here. With the open-ended approach, can find any pattern at any generation. With the SGD approach, you can only look for one pattern. So it's just not an apples to apples comparison and sort of misleading / unfair to say that open-endedness is way more "efficient", because you aren't asking it to do the same task. the open-endedness looking for thousands millions) of shapes simultaneously. With SGD you're kinda flipping that around, and looking for exactly 1 shape, but giving it thousands of generations to achieve it. Earlier discussion: A deep dive into self-improving AI and the Darwin-Gödel Machine https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44174856 Theoretically it is nice. We did the same in the 80's for evolving small NN (less than 30 neurons) for controlling self sustaining simulated mobile robots. and less good at fine Hmm, it's more that LLMs can be used for population -> candidate solution generation, e.g. operators in a GA. The innovation is novelty search, e.g. divergent rather than convergent optimization, paired with the capability that LLM genetic operators and representations unlock. . google's alpha ve is the same kind of thing but focused on convergent ga's (i think). So it's basically "throw spaghetti at the wall and see what sticks". It works in evolution because evolution doesn't have an end goal to achieve in a certain amount of time, but for AI we want to know how long it takes to go from performance A to B. Then again, this paper might be yet another validation of the bitter truth of machine learning.
